newsitem.title: UK: Genoa airport criticised over bird strike problem.
newsitem.headline: Genoa airport criticised over bird strike problem.

text.p: Genoa airport has been strongly criticised by Antonov Design Bureau (ADB) for allegedly not doing enough to resolve a serious bird strike problem.
Ukraine-based ADB also said the airport did not send fire truck support to help of one of its giant AN-124 freighters hit by about 50 large seagulls after taking off from the airport on June 19.

"It cost in excess of $10 million to repair the damage," and to fly in a Boeing 747 freighter and an AN-22F to reposition the cargo to Milan, said a spokesman for ADB's worldwide management agent, Air Foyle.
But the airport authority has told Reuters that bird strike prevention measures were in force at the time of the take-off. A full commercial load of turbines and spares bound for Karachi was aboard.
It added that the pilot did not give the control tower a distress call after the collision and therefore emergency procedures were not activated when the plane landed, after 11 minutes.

Air Foyle said that after being cleared for take off, the 140-tonne capacity plane -- the world's biggest commercially used freighter -- hit the seagulls, which flew up from long grass. Most of the birds were killed and blood splatttered over the plane's frontage.
It said the nose and all four engines of the plane were damaged and one had to be shut down before an emergency landing was made.

"The airport authority provided no fire truck, has charged us the full rate for any services provided, such as parking, and has taken no responsibility for the incident. They have washed their hands of it," he said.
He added that although the airport claimed its bird scaring device adequately did its job, "this is clearly not the case".
Air Foyle chairman Chris Foyle that the June 19 bird strike "was not an isolated incident" at the airport.
"I would really like them to do something about this problem. Their response to us is that they couldn't give a damn but they would if it were a passenger-related incident," he said.
The Genoa airport authority said in a statement it had been having seagull problems for 10 years and had four bird scaring devices in force.
It stressed that legally, once aircraft had taken off from Genoa it was the responsibility of Italy's civil aviation general management (Civilavia), not the airport authority.
It added that the authority emphasised to airlines that they must by law be insured against bird strikes.
